figure.name: Mao Zedong
figure.role: Chinese Communist leader associated with rural revolution, party rule, mass campaigns, land struggle, and state-led transformation.
figure.hook: Mao = Marxism-Leninism adapted to rural revolution and mass mobilization.
whyHere: Mao belongs here because Marxism-Leninism changes when it is adapted to a largely rural society, peasant revolution, land struggle, civil war, and Chinese state-building.
He matters because the global socialism/communism map cannot be only European, Russian, or American. China becomes one of the major twentieth-century test cases.
figure.cleanIdea: Mao's road asks how revolutionary theory changes when peasants, land, party organization, military struggle, and mass campaigns become central.

ideas.title: Maoism
ideas.plainDefinition: Maoism is a Marxist-Leninist current shaped by Chinese revolutionary experience, rural struggle, party organization, military strategy, and mass mobilization.
ideas.context: In the Mao path, Marxism-Leninism is adapted to a different social setting from industrial Europe.
ideas.whyMatters: Maoism matters because it shows socialism and communism became global languages with different national and social forms.

ideas.title: Peasant Revolution
ideas.plainDefinition: Peasant revolution means revolutionary politics centered on rural populations, land struggle, village organization, and agrarian power.
ideas.context: In the Mao path, peasants are not treated as a side issue. They become central to revolution and state-building.
ideas.whyMatters: Peasant revolution matters because it changes the map from factory-only socialism to land, countryside, and colonial or semi-colonial conditions.

ideas.title: Mass Campaigns
ideas.plainDefinition: Mass campaigns are organized political drives meant to mobilize large numbers of people around state, party, or ideological goals.
ideas.context: In the Mao path, mass campaigns become a governing method as well as a revolutionary method.
ideas.whyMatters: Mass campaigns matter because they show how political participation, mobilization, pressure, and state direction can overlap.
